Chapter Four: Rethinking Productivity and Measurement
So, let’s talk about how we usually think about productivity. Most organizations zero in on keeping everyone and everything busy—pushing for maximum output at every step, and cutting costs wherever they can. Now, on the surface, that sounds like a solid plan, right? But here’s the catch: those metrics can actually push teams in the wrong direction, leading to behaviors that end up hurting the whole system.
Picture this—a factory where each department gets rewarded for cranking out as many parts as possible, even if those parts aren’t needed right away. What happens? You get stacks of extra inventory sitting around, tying up cash, taking up space, and making it harder to respond when real customer demand comes in. Or maybe someone’s laser-focused on cutting operating costs in one area, but that means other critical resources start to dry up, slowing everything down.
The real question is: what if we measured success by the system’s ability to achieve its true goal—making money by delivering value to customers? That’s where a new way of thinking comes in. Instead of old-school metrics, we focus on three big ones:
First, Throughput—that’s the rate at which your system actually generates money, not just by producing stuff, but through real sales.
Second, Inventory—this is all the money tied up in materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods.
And third, Operating Expense—the ongoing costs you need to turn that inventory into throughput.
When you track these three measures, you can start to see how changes in one spot ripple across the whole business. For example, if you boost throughput by selling more products, that’s fantastic—unless it means you’ve had to pile up way more inventory or ramp up expenses just to keep up. And sure, reducing inventory frees up cash and gives you more flexibility, but not if it causes shortages that slow down your entire flow. Cutting operating expenses sounds great, but if it creates bottlenecks that choke output, you’re just shooting yourself in the foot.
This is where the idea of flow comes in—the smooth movement of materials and information through your system. Whenever flow gets blocked, inventory piles up, costs climb, and customers end up waiting longer for what they need. By putting flow at the center, you can spot the real causes of delays and inefficiency, and tackle them head-on.
To really make this work, simple, visual tools can be a big help. Imagine a chart that shows where inventory is building up at different steps—suddenly, bottlenecks become crystal clear. Or a quick daily report on throughput, inventory, and operating expense—it gives managers a real-time snapshot of how their decisions are playing out.
What’s powerful about this approach is that it shifts everyone’s focus. Instead of rewarding local efficiency or just keeping busy, it gets teams working together on the bigger picture: delivering real value to customers, making money, and keeping the organization healthy for the long haul.
Plus, it sparks a culture of continuous improvement. By regularly checking these key measures, teams can spot new constraints, try out solutions, and actually learn from what happens. The whole mindset shifts away from blame and finger-pointing, and moves toward solving problems together.
So, here’s the key takeaway: rethinking productivity and measurement means looking past those traditional metrics. When you align what you measure with your real goals, teams make smarter decisions, move faster when things change, and build a business that’s stronger and more adaptable than ever.
